mcqs.question: Why can five small, chatty API requests actually cost a mobile device more battery than one larger consolidated request, even at the same total byte count?
options: Every network request wakes the device's radio, and that wake cost is paid per request regardless of how much data each one transfers
Small requests always take longer to process on the server than large ones
Mobile devices cannot make more than one network request per second
Battery cost is purely a function of total bytes transferred, unrelated to request count
mcqs.explanation: Radio wake-up has a real, largely fixed battery cost per request, so five separate requests pay that cost five times over even if the combined payload size matches one larger request — this is exactly why request count, not just payload size, matters for mobile battery. There's no per-second request cap, and battery cost is not purely proportional to bytes transferred.

mcqs.question: A mobile profile header screen only displays a user's name and avatar, but calls a generic /users/{id} endpoint that returns the full user object including bio, settings, and internal admin flags. What does payload shaping recommend here?
options: Continue using the generic endpoint but ignore the extra fields client-side, since network cost doesn't matter once data arrives
Cache the full response locally so the extra fields are only downloaded once per app install
Switch the entire app to GraphQL, since REST cannot support payload shaping at all
Have the BFF or a screen-specific endpoint return only name and avatar URL, avoiding downloading and discarding fields the screen never renders
mcqs.explanation: Payload shaping's core discipline is not making the mobile client download data it never renders — a screen-specific endpoint or BFF response tailored to just name and avatar directly achieves this. Ignoring extra fields after download still pays the transfer cost, caching doesn't address the per-request waste, and REST-based BFFs can achieve the same effect as GraphQL through screen-specific endpoints.

mcqs.question: A company has iOS, Android, and web clients with very similar data needs on iOS and Android but a meaningfully different one on web. What's a reasonable BFF granularity choice?
options: Three fully separate BFFs, one per platform, regardless of how similar iOS and Android's needs are
One shared BFF for iOS and Android, separate from web's BFF or general API, since the mobile platforms' needs are much more similar to each other than to web's
One single general-purpose API for all three clients, since BFFs are never worth the added complexity
No BFF at all — mobile clients should always call backend services directly
mcqs.explanation: BFF granularity should match how divergent each client's actual needs are — since iOS and Android's needs are described as similar here, one shared mobile BFF avoids duplicating nearly identical logic across two BFFs, while web's genuinely different needs justify its own. Three separate BFFs would duplicate near-identical logic, and both 'always one general API' and 'never a BFF' ignore that the right granularity is context-dependent.

mcqs.question: A team wants to remove a field from an existing API response shape that a meaningful percentage of active users' app versions still parse and depend on. What's the recommended approach?
options: Remove the field immediately, since the backend team controls the API and should not be blocked by old clients
Only remove it during a scheduled maintenance window to minimize visible impact
Add a new versioned endpoint or version alongside the old one, and use real version-adoption telemetry to determine when it's actually safe to sunset the old shape
Silently ignore the concern, since mobile OS app stores force all users onto the latest version automatically
mcqs.explanation: Because a real percentage of users can be running old app versions indefinitely, removing a field they depend on requires versioning and a deprecation window informed by actual adoption data, not an assumption that everyone updates. Removing it immediately or during a maintenance window doesn't change the fact that old clients would break, and app stores do not force automatic updates on all users.

mcqs.question: A mobile screen makes five sequential API calls directly to five different backend services to assemble its data. On a high-latency cellular connection, what's the primary cost of this pattern?
options: The calls are guaranteed to fail entirely on cellular connections
Each round trip's latency is paid individually and can add up to a full second or more of visible loading before the screen is usable
This pattern has no meaningful cost difference from a single aggregated request
The five calls will always execute in parallel automatically, so latency doesn't compound
mcqs.explanation: Sequential round trips on a high-latency connection compound additively, and each one crosses the client's slow, variable mobile connection independently — a BFF aggregating them server-side, where services are close together on a fast internal network, avoids paying that cost per call from the client. The calls don't fail outright on cellular, aren't cost-free, and don't automatically parallelize unless the client code is specifically written to do so.

mcqs.question: A backend team changes a response field's type from a string ID to a numeric ID without versioning the change. What's the likely effect on users running an older app version?
options: No effect — clients always gracefully adapt to a changed field type automatically
The old app version will automatically download the new parsing logic over the air
This only affects users on the very latest app version, not older ones
The change can cause old clients' parsing code to fail, sometimes as a hard crash and sometimes as silently missing data
mcqs.explanation: Changing an existing field's type is a breaking change to the response contract, and old clients whose parsing code expects the original type can crash on parse or silently fail to read the field, since there's no automatic adaptation or over-the-air logic update for shipped app binaries. This risk applies specifically to clients running versions predating the change, not the latest one.
